Editor's Introduction

Elizabeth Dorsey MSW

Elizabeth Dorsey

6 Beach Road
Gloucester, MA 01930

Elizabeth Dorsey   Faculty member, training analyst and supervising analyst at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis. She is the coordinator of the BGSP Annual Cape Cod Summer Institute. She conducts private practice in Gloucester and Brookline, MA.

The papers that appear in this issue were presented at the Annual Cape Cod Summer Institute of the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis, held August 2-9, 1997, in Wellfleet, Massachusetts. The program, entitled Becoming Themselves: What Kids Really Need, brought together conferees from the United States and abroad with modern psychoanalysts and guest speakers to examine the interaction of temperament and environment in the course of development.

The Summer Institute celebrated its thirteenth session, the tenth year welcoming health care professionals, educators, students, youth workers, court and law enforcement personnel, social scientists, parents, community members, and others interested in learning about psychoanalytic knowledge and its applications. Early meetings were co-sponsored with other training institutes, including the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. Psychoanalytic educators gathered to review and enhance curriculum, develop teaching methods, and establish standards for instructional programs in the United States. (See Vol. XIII, No. 2, Emotional Education: The Theory and Process of Training Psychoanalysts.)

The Institute provides an annual forum for psychoanalysts, students of psychoanalysis, and the broader academic and social community.

Becoming Themselves: What Kids Really Need begins with a modern psychoanalytic introduction by Phyllis Meadow to the study of biological and psychic functioning at the formative stages of life.

Joanne White MSW

Joanne White

1583 Beacon Street
Brookline, MA 02146

Joanne White   Certified psychoanalyst. She serves on the faculty and is a training and supervising analyst at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis. She is the coordinator of the Substance Abuse Program at the Lynn Community Health Center and is a consultant to the Lynn Public School System.

This paper examines conflicts of adolescence, a time when the intensity of drives exacerbated by hormonal influx and a weakened defense system disturb psychic balance. At this maturational stage, the adolescent's constitutional and genetic factors become evident in the adolescent's ability to withstand the disturbances. Two cases that illustrate two poles of adolescent acting out are presented. If the acting out is environmentally induced, libido will triumph. If the acting out is under the dominance of the destructive drive and there are no sustaining emotional memories, there is only immediate gratification and no future; self-destruction may predominate.

In the Beginning: The Contribution of Temperament to Personality Development

Jerome Kagan PHD

Jerome Kagan

Cambridge, MA 02138

Jerome Kagan   Professor of psychology at Harvard University who for years has conducted research on child and adolescent temperament. He is author of numerous articles and books, including The Nature of the Child and Understanding Children. His latest book is Galen's Prophecy.

This paper summarizes developmental research on two temperamental types: inhibited and uninhibited measured in terms of reactivity to stimulation. The research indicates that a biological basis exists for these two temperamental types and that these traits remain stable during the childhood years. Though there is a biological foundation to temperament, environmental factors do exert influence.

This article discusses some of the considerations necessary for determining who needs psychoanalysis and when it should be used in conjunction with other modes of intervention. Clinical case material is used to illustrate particular kinds of patients who may need interventions in addition to psychoanalysis, such as those whose destructive wishes are being acted on in ways that are more gratifying than the process of talking would be. In addition, the paper offers comments on the presentations which were presented on days prior to this one at the 1997 Annual Cape Cod Conference, specifically on subjects like Kagan's research about high-reactive temperament in infants, the pros and cons of self-analysis, and the problem of separation of mother and child as it relates to the ability to use aggression constructively.

Jane Goldberg   Private practice in New York City and northern New Jersey. She is on the faculty of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies and the Psychoanalytic Center for Northern New Jersey. She has authored numerous articles and has lectured widely in the fields of experimental psychology, psychoanalysis, and psychological oncology. The author uses her experience as a mother of a young child to understand the preoedipal needs of children. Paramount among what children need is the mother's sensitivity to creating an emotional environment which balances the conflicting needs for union and separation. Recent research is presented delineating findings on the importance of touch, aspects of the development of language, the impact of the communication of emotions as well as the use of emotions in the development of cognition, and, finally, the role and importance of the father in the development of the ego.

This book is a masterful presentation by a brilliant psychoanalyst. McDougall describes her theories in meticulous detail followed by detailed case presentations illustrating their derivation and use. However, she cautions us that clinical vignettes prove nothing: they only illustrate a theoretical conception.

The work is mainly focused on the atypical expressions of sex when sex has been infiltrated with misconceptions, hatred and fear. The sexual patterns that ensue when psychic integrity is threatened are seen as the helpless infant's primitive, unconscious life saving inventions that persist in every adult. She urges us to recognize their origins and importance for the survival of the patient.

McDougall starts by giving us the current psychoanalytic view of woman's sexual development.

Letter to Freud

B. Margolis

B. Margolis

B. Margolis  

Dear Professor: Your ashes in the grecian urn,

courtesy Marie Bonaparte, bear

no autograph. They could be Jung's,

Ferenczi's, particles lacking Lust-Unlust,

rising from your signature cigar.

Your absence compels an image. You will be sighted,

not Elvis Presley-like driving a white Cadillac,

but meditating in your book-lined study

on Berggasse 19, with Horus, Isis, Aphrodite,

and all the other goddesses

Sandra Augustinho M.Ed.

Sandra Augustinho

2308 Highland Avenue
Fall River, MA 02720

Sandra Augustinho   Special Educator in the Fall River, MA public school system. She is currently a student in the Extension Division at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis.

School failure at the beginning of elementary school today may result in referral of children to special education classrooms. The teacher uses knowledge of maturational needs of the age group to prepare an intellectually and emotionally nourishing environment for the group and for the individual youngsters. The length of time a class remains together, with the adult leadership, may be an important factor of the development of successful learning patterns. Likewise, a single, particularly needy child requires a constant environment for an extended period, in order to alter destructive actions and states. The author's work with a three-year core group and with one deeply troubled student demonstrate the benefits of a developmental timeframe.

The Talking Cure: The Science Behind PsychotherapySusan C. Vaughan. New York: G.P. Putnam's Sons, 1997. 208 pp.

Steven Poser

Steven Poser

Steven Poser  

The central thesis of this book, announced in the opening pages with something approaching messianic fervor, is that psychoanalysis changes your brain—that intensive psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy is, quite literally, a kind of neurosurgery in which interconnections among neurons in the brain are re-wired, bringing about permanent alterations in the way the patient thinks, feels, acts, and relates to others. “I am a microsurgeon of the mind,” proclaims Vaughan. “A physician psychiatrist, and psychoanalyst by training, I use words and symbols to explore and change the neural landscape of my patients' mind and brains the way a surgeon uses a scalpel to expose and excise problematic structures in the body” (p. 3). Her purpose in this book is to show how and why she can make this claim:

Let me say at the outset that in calling psychotherapy neurosurgery, I am not speaking metaphorically. We now have solid scientific evidence to suggest that the so-called “talking cure,” originally devised by Freud, literally alters the way in which the neurons in the brain are connected to one another….

Barbara Socor has written a very good book. It is lucid, even when exploring some abstruse and opaque regions of psychoanalytic thought. It is ambitious, taking on the major theorists of the ego and the self. It is focused, telling the story of psychoanalysis from the well-defined vantage point of the epistemologies implicit in the underlying concepts of presence and absence. It is reflective, displaying a sound and subtly nuanced grasp of the fundamental philosophical and psychoanalytic concepts around which the basic theme of the work is formulated.

Jack Burlison

Jack Burlison  

“As-if pathology is essentially imitative, a way of life built on an endless series of transient identifications in which the individual acts as if he or she were sensitive, empathic, conservative, religious, or even rebellious—all dependent on what others want the individual to be” (p. xiii). This definition would find acceptance from Helena Deutsch (1942) who first introduced the topic. She became interested in a type of pathology she observed that “should” have produced psychosis or schizophrenia, but did not. Little has been written on the subject since. Thus the intention of the present authors, who attempt to elaborate on the subject, since they believe there to be a great many more patients of this type than are written about.

The authors place the as-if “phenomena” on a continuum and call in the “quiet borderline.” This places these patients in the “borderline” category diagnostically. They are “quiet” in contrast to the “noisy” borderline patients about which there is much written. By “quiet” the authors point out that there is an appearance of normalcy and an unwillingness to be in conflict with the environment, an avoidance of feelings of weakness or dependency, excessive passivity and severe identity problems. They believe this not to be defensive in nature and the “as-if” person not to be schizoid.

Etiology is explained from the viewpoint of internalized object relations. The relationship between the child and the mother in the first three or four years of life is the focus. A further interactive perspective used to explain etiology is family interaction. The stress is on what happens in the individual's social world. The authors use the second perspective to explain the first. There is an absence of any attempt to explain the as-if personality through a study of the drives.

Lorraine Smithberg PHD

Lorraine Smithberg

460 West 24th Street, #1A
New York, NY 10011

Lorraine Smithberg   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York and Brookline, MA. She serves on the faculty and is a training and supervising analyst at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies and the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis,

The title of this conference implies we know “what kids really need.” At this moment many of us are struggling to integrate complex concepts which often seem at odds. In this conference we, as analysts and educators, are pondering the role of drives and their contribution to learning. Meadow in her comments referred to “the biological bases of behavior.” She cited “the need to make helplessness tolerable” and presented an understanding of mental development as “an attempt to control tension.”

What implications do such concepts have for teaching, for parenting, for training of practitioners? The following authors will address their question of enactment based on our best knowledge to date of what children need.

As a background for these presentations I will now briefly outline my own guiding concepts in my work with children, families and those who help them. Children need maturational competency in three areas:

to know what they feel, to be able to tolerate what they feel, to be able to perceive what others feel, to tolerate what others feel;

to ask for what they want, to learn how to get it constructively and creatively, and to tolerate not getting it;

to discover what they can do, what they can say, what they can trust.

Learning to Work with Children

Jennifer Andrews MA

Jennifer Andrews

PO Box 324
Thetford Center, VT 05075

Jennifer Andrews   Special Educator in Vershire, VT Elementary School. She is the first recipient of the Master of Arts in Psychoanalysis at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanlaysis and is a certificate candidate in BGSP's Institute of Psychoanalysis.

When a child's behavior is overwhelming to adults, s/he is often seen as “manipulative.” In fact the child's defenses are apparent in actions that are disruptive to maturational and learning processes. Understanding the symbolic meaning of the behavior provides the tools for a constructive response in the classroom, where the goal is to resolve resistances to cognitive and social development. The author presents three cases, in which the teacher used her awareness of emotional blocks to participation in the educational setting to respond to flight and oppositional behaviors. The use of fairy tales, feelingful joining and mirroring, and persistent personal presence led to verbal communication between teacher and student and increased cooperation.

The first briefly examines the psychology of totalism as it affects cults and extremist groups all over the world, but especially extremist religious cults and cults more prone to apocalyptic violence. Phyllis Meadow

Phyllis Meadow   Founder and Chair of the Board of Trustees of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies and the President of the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis. She is Editor of this journal, and founder and former President of the Society of Modern Psychoanalysts. She has published numerous articles on drive theory and psychoanalytic research and is author of the monograph, Emotional Education: The Theory and Process of Training Psychoanalysts, co-author of the book, Treatment of the Narcissistic Neuroses. A monograph of her selected papers, Phyllis W. Meadow: Selected Theoretical and Clinical Papers was recently published by this journal.

Violence is as old as humankind. Freud late in his life postulated the presence of an innate aggressive drive. Violence is not just learned. It is innate and seeks discharge. History shows how each of us uses relations with family, friends and educators to learn the ways provided by our society and culture for the expression of destructive urges. Freud's drive theory gave us a way to view the consequences when aggression is impeded from discharge. Freud (1933) wrote, “It really seems necessary for us to destroy some other thing or person in order not to destroy ourselves, in order to guard against the impulsion to self-destruct” (p. 105). The question is how the aggressive drive is channeled. For psychoanalysis, the question is pertinent. “Can it affect the problems created when men turn their innate aggression into actions directed against each other?” Modern psychoanalysis has developed techniques and a theory for working with destructive impulsivity.

For treatment to succeed, analyst and patient agree on constructive goals. Analysts have the right to discharge patients who are unwilling to accept constructive goals. It is also the analyst's prerogative not to work with patients who have a history of violence where there is danger that violent behavior will occur in the analytic relationship. Preverbal resistances require providing patients with emotional experiences, and the analyst should be prepared to surrender his ego in the service of understanding the patient on a sensori-somatic level. Analysis, however, has the potential for doing harm as well as good. It is possible that analysis may have toxic results both for analyst and patient. Research is needed to discover which ways of being with patients help them to grow and avoid undesirable outcomes, somatization among them.

Louis Ormont PHD

Louis Ormont

Louis Ormont   Director of the Center for the Advancement of Group Studies and clinical professor at the Gordon Derner Institute of Advanced Studies in Psychotherapy, Adelphi University. He is author of The Group Therapy Experience and numerous papers on group analysis.

The author identifies the main distinctions between modern group analysis and preceding methods of group therapy. Traditionally, the therapist focused on individuals in turn, with the rest acting as assistants. In modern group analysis, the analyst turns the group into the agent of change. Converting the group into the therapeutic agent requires specific interventions. The modern group analyst is primarily concerned with preserving and enhancing themes that arise in the room, always emphasizing emotional communication rather than insights. This paper discusses some concepts that are fundamental to modern group analysis. The chief one is the technique of bridging—methods of linking members of a group together in feeling and outlook. A second is helping a whole group meet the maturational needs of its members. Other techniques include developing the members' insulation barriers and cultivating their observing egos.

This is an investigation of what the motives are that lead the patient to devalue the analyst. The results indicate that devaluing serves as a means of discharge for her sadism and aggression, as a defense against awareness of self-hatred and longing for closeness, and as a distancing maneuver that interferes with the direct expression of specific negative images. On a deeper level, the patient's devaluation of the analyst represents a devaluation of parts of herself which she has not succeeded in integrating into her personality.

Robert Wallerstein has been a major voice in psychoanalysis for the last thirty years. His work as the principal investigator of the thirty-five year long Psychotherapy Research Project of the Menninger Foundation, the results of which were published in 1986, is well known. In addition, he has written extensively about research and technique and about practically every theoretical development in psychoanalysis. His approach is consistently balanced and fair, and indicative of a wide range of experience and a significant depth of understanding.

The subtitle of The Talking Cures, “The Psychoanalyses and the Psychotherapies,” reveals the principal goal of the book, which is to study the emergence of these multiple and diverse developments from what appeared at one time to be a consensus of uniformity, i.e., from a univocally intelligible psychoanalysis. As Wallerstein observes, however, such a uniform understanding was always only putative at best. In the early years, dissidents were simply expelled to preserve the purity of psychoanalysis and their views were deemed alien to its nature and purposes, only to be reintegrated over the decades following. The conflict between the Kleinians and the Anna Freudians in Britain culminated not in expulsions but in accommodation and in the practical acceptance of some theoretical diversity.

A major technical problem in treating paranoid patients is establishment of a working alliance. Most paranoids come to treatment with a monumental chip balanced precariously on their shoulders, and almost any remark of the analyst's may dislodge that chip. Every utterance is taken as a demonstration of the analyst's incapacity to treat the patient. I am emphasizing this opening phase of the treatment of paranoids, because unless one can keep these patients in treatment, it is impossible to help them.

Once the transferential glue has set and the analysis is ready to begin, one of the questions raised in this book by Auchincloss and Weiss becomes very valuable, how to understand the alternation, within patients, and even within a session, of persecuting ideation with blissful euphoria. Their explanation is particularly satisfying, since it does not offer a single answer, but rather indicates a strategy of questioning, the result of which will result in the patient doing a lot more talking, which, as w are beginning to understand, is what we want to happen in analysis.

Further on in the same chapter Auchincloss and Weiss make the point that:

… it was necessary to interpret derivatives of and defenses against primitive oral aggression and envy so that object constancy could be established and intimate relationships tolerated.

The so-called “reality principle,”—acting in accordance with predictable consequences rather than just immediate pleasure or discharge—requires the ability to fantasize. There are several environmental (“nurture”) factors which contribute to the successful development of this ability. These are: an abundance of pleasurable experiences which can be anticipated; a moderate number of adverse events, which have been “detoxified” by their association with emotional support; and, in addition, exposure to vicarious experiences, but only according to the same rules—that is, such experiences should be primarily positive, and if negative, then associated with a positive emotional context.

Susan Lynaugh   Certified psychoanalyst and psychologist for the Ridgewood New Jersey public school system.

In the competitive world of school, experiences of success motivate children to learn and achieve in the classroom. Resistance to learning in the form of disruptive behavior, inattentiveness, failure to complete work, and lack of motivation often result from the child's experience of failure or excessive frustration in learning. Academic success requires intact ego functions which continue to develop through the learning and mastery experiences provided in the classroom. These ego functions are described from the educational and neurological viewpoint by Marvin Levine as neurodevelopmental constructs such as attention, memory, and sequencing ability which constitute the components of the ability to learn. Thorough investigation of the child's cognitive and learning profile is essential in order to identify possible reasons for academic difficulty. Emotional stress from family or other sources can also impair ego functioning, causing blocks to learning which lead to resistance in the classroom. Once the source of the learning difficulty is clear, appropriate interventions can often effectively address problem behaviors.

Bill Stewart   Assistant Chief Probation Officer in Dorchester, MA District Court. He is the creator of Operation Night Light, Boston's high impact street intervention with violent young people. The model program has now been adopted in cities nationwide.

The influx of “crack” cocaine led to the growth of the 1980's street gang culture in America's cities. Along with drug use, abuse, and trafficking came abundant firearms and escalating violence. Juvenile homicides and armed assaults spiraled, as gang members became entrenched in a repetitive cycle of destruction. In Boston, probation officer Bill Stewart observed the failure of conventional office practice to influence individual youths whose dangerous lifestyle promised death or long incarceration. Moving into the streets, using gang language and style, his team learned that the large majority of gang members were motivated, at some level, to respond to believable authority. More demanding terms of probation, notably curfews and association rules for offenders, and nightime street presence backed by police have changed the impact of department's work. The combination of mentoring and enforcement, along with authentic use of the probation officer's personality, creates the opportunity for violent young people to communicate with the officer and to make constructive choices.

What It Means to Be a Healthy Child

Thomas Lynaugh PHD

Thomas Lynaugh

1583 Beacon Street
Brookline, MA 02146

Thomas Lynaugh   Professor of Psychoanalysis at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis and a training and supervising analyst at BGSP's Institute for Psychoanalytic Studies.

Cultural pressures to raise superior children committed to endless self-improvement, and psychic pressures to avoid both our own feelings of helplessness and aloneness and our children's hatred and death wishes toward us interfere with our ability to understand what it means to be a healthy child. The concept of temperament has significant implications for an understanding of psychic health in children. A child is not unhealthy just because he is difficult to manage. Understanding and tolerating the wide range of temperamental differences in children leads to a focus on channeling the expression of impulses rather than inhibiting them. A definition of the healthy child is offered for discusion.

The Psychic Life of Power: Theories in Subjection. Judith Butler. Stanford, CA: Stanford University Press, 1997. 215 pp.

Elaine Hurst

Elaine Hurst

Elaine Hurst  

Stated succinctly, Judith Butler's central insight seems deceptively simple: the emergence of self-consciousness is rooted in paradox—for becoming a subject is intricately bound up with being subjected. This insight, which Butler ascribes to Foucault, is explored and developed as her book unfolds, taking the reader through a tour de force of its rhetorical, linguistic, philosophical, psychoanalytic, and social and political implications. Butler, a professor of rhetoric and comparative literature at Berkeley, focuses on the paradoxical self-assertion and awareness of subjection which takes place when self-consciousness arises—the “self,” in a sense, both accepting and renouncing those external forces which exert power over it, in the very process of defining itself as an empowered subject. This involves a “turning in upon itself” which Butler compares to the rhetorical device of the “trope”—a stylistic deviation from the ordinary, logical use of language, which does, nonetheless, generate a new understanding, through a kind of turning or twisting of words or images. As such, a trope is a type of performative utterance—constitutive, rather than descriptive in its function. As Butler duly acknowledges, the “tropological” formation of the subject, giving rise to questions such as: “What or who is said to turn, and what is the object of such a turn?” (p. 4), obviates the possibility of describing the origins of self-consciousness in clear, unambiguous language. Thus, the reader looking for simple, easy characterizations of the formation of the self will not find them in this book.

What the reader will find who does perservere through the author's difficult, and sometimes perhaps unnecessarily obscure language, is a rather thought-provoking study of the process of becoming a subject—as Butler examines the theoretical approaches of the 19th century philosophers, Hegel and Nietzsche, linking their insights with those of Freud and Lacan, as well as the social theories of Foucault and Althusser. Finally, she reflects upon the melancholy, ambivalence, and rage which arise when self-identities are formed—focusing specifically on the psychoanalytic and sociocultural ramifications of the establishment of heterosexual or homosexual “identities.
